speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Alright, my name is Clay Adkins. I’m the research director for the Calfee Center right down the road from where we are today. We’re at the First Baptist Church in Pulaski, Virginia. Today is June 14th, 2026, and I’m sitting here with.

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: Natasha Grubb.

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: And Randy Grubb

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Thank you for agreeing to sit down with me today and be interviewed… So, I’m wondering how long you all have attended the First Baptist Church [on Magazine Street].

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: Hmmm...? [inaudible]

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: How long have we been here? My dad is the pastor. So, since he became Pastor, that’s when we started coming here

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Okay. And where did you attend before?

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: he had a church in… Woodlawn… [inaudible] it’s a small area… and so he was there before, so. Yeah, I guess before that it was Pentecostal Holiness Church… like on Johnson...? I guess it’s on Johnson Street

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: So, what has that been like? Your dad being the pastor, what’s that like?

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: It’s a lot; it’s a lot, you know, like how everybody interacts, and it’s a little different when you’re the preacher’s family, and you know.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: It’s kind of like when your parents are a teacher or something.

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: Yeah… Yeah

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: I guess when the pastor is like your father-in-law or dad, it’s almost like if your son is the quarterback for the football team, you know what I’m saying? [inaudible] It's cool and helpful to me

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: So, what’s it like the music, we're really focused on the music; how gospel music brings people together… so what would you… what’s your fondest memory of gospel music here in the church or any of the churches?

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: I mean it’s cool um [inaudible] it’s similar to he church I attended as a kid and you know the church that we went to in Woodlawn; and the ones that we like between this church and Woodlawn; he was preaching at a couple different churches like you know the church in Dublin and another church in Pulaski just you know trying to fill in till getting another job. So it’s all good; it gets the day going and gets like the spirit going, you know what I mean.

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: Yes, it definitely makes a difference since [inaudible] music is good; it makes the whole service

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Yes, I get what you’re saying, so are you all from Pulaski originally?

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: Yes, I’m from Pulaski

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: I’m from New River

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Okay, and where did each of you go to school?

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: We went to Pulaski County High School

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Okay, and what year did you all graduate

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: What was it like going to Pulaski [County High School]. Usually I’ll talk to older folks, but I’m curious what it’s like…more recent.

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: And I’ve also worked there recently [inaudible]… I went to Pulaski County High School and then after, I guess it was still during COVID… So, when schools were fresh back open, I worked there at Pulaski County High School. I worked there like a year and a half or something like that. It wasn’t too much off of, you know… I don’t think… now in Pulaski County Schools is too much off of when it was integrated, you know what I mean. I don’t think that it was much different, you know, when we went to school to then and to now. I mean it’s all the same people and all the same names that you see, and I ain’t trying to bash nobody or nothing, but you know what I mean. [Inaudible] they just want to keep it all the same, you know what I mean. I mean we don’t have our kids, we live in Dublin, and we don’t have our kids going to Pulaski County Schools. So no, I don’t think I would send a kid there.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Yeah, I have a follow-up to that, and so some of the work we’ve investigated at the Calfee Center is that there were more Black teachers before integration than there are after. How many Black teachers do you recall when you went through Pulaski County? Were there none?

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: There was none at the high school, were there?

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: Yeah, yeah, yeah, there was, when we was in high school it was one that was a Principal, and he had been a teacher, and I think that is it. And then when I was in middle school in Dublin, there was two Black teachers. Man, I think that’s probably it, and then there was like one in elementary school in Pulaski but, that was… that was all.. Now it ain’t… it is the same, [inaudible] now it might be three in the high school and a Black janitor maybe… or two or three and a Black janitor and that’s it. And they don’t want it to change; they want to keep it the same. They don’t want that to change… You know you can kind of like suppress people; you know, just beat ‘em down, man.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: So, what has kept you in Pulaski? You know you’ve got some criticisms I get, you know, but what has kept you here

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: Family… Family, I mean if it wasn’t for that we probably we have been done moved. I mean my mom is still here, her dad is still here. Her mom just passed away a couple years ago, so that was kind of you know… her mom was dealing with like sickness for fifteen to sixteen years, so you know what I mean she was here for them and now we’re here to support her dad and to support my mom and my aunts you know everybody’s getting older so we’re just here to kind of support them; and I mean… Our kids don’t go to Pulaski County Schools, but you know my daughter goes to Radford, my son goes to Roanoke Catholic. I mean once he’s out of school, I mean we’ll probably have to… Probably leave, you know what I mean. As a family, we’ve kind of outgrown Pulaski County, and we see that as it might be time to go; and kind of broaden yourself.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: What do you mean by outgrowing Pulaski?

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: That is just a very slow place with not much going on, you know what I mean. And then we go to Roanoke every day, and we see stuff like growing up we see something every day you see things growing, you know there just ain’t much going on here. And it’s just, you know, you come home to the same neighborhood [inaudible] nice and quiet, which is cool, but then you know it’s just trying to get… do better things and just see more

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: It’s not a lot here… for younger people

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: It’s not a lot here… and when it is, it doesn’t last long. I mean nothing lasts too long here. It’s a pretty depressing place at some times.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: But what about the community you get from the Church, and how does that kind of help you even though outside of these walls or outside of your family it’s a little more challenging. How does the community of the church support you?

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: I think it I mean, I feel like we’re family, and we help each other whenever we need to do anything; we all work together. It's good; it’s like family, you know. And I don’t want to be like, you know, everything is all bad and gloomy… but I know it did come off that way a little bit, but I know like with his job he works a lot within the community, in the school’s systems, and he sees a lot that’s in the school system and how it works. Here it’s just, you know…

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: Church is cool… It’s like a family, a lot of love.

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: And you know, especially since my mom passed, it seems like we’ve grown closer as a family... church family.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: A church family, yeah, I got what you said. So, I guess I’ll ask this question and then leave space for if you all want to share any stories or favorite memories from church or growing up here in Pulaski or anything like that. But what do you think here at the Calfee Center, [inaudible] trying to revitalize Pulaski in some regards, and build community maybe where community struggles to be built at times. So, what would you think the Calfee Center or another organization can do to improve Pulaski… that’s kind of vague, but a way to give you that sense that you haven’t outgrown it [Pulaski]?

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: Right… it just kind of needs to do stuff for like kids… I mean, or it’s just going to be the same. It has to be somewhere for youth to tap into something that they’re not getting at home… they’re not getting at school… it has to be something like that, or it’s not going to last. It can’t be the same cycle, you know… can’t be like, " Oh, my mom and dad are a drug user so man I'm gonna have to come up and be a drug user that’s a lot that I see. Kids tell me that while working in the schools, like they just have no hope; they really think they’re gonna be drug users; just because of how they were raised. That they might have a kid and not have the dad around because that is what happened to them. You know what I mean? It’s just the youth have to know there is more than walking around Pulaski; they gotta know that. There's more than these… when you’re walking around, stores are broken down, and busted windows, stuff like that. It has to be more than that, than abandoned… like this street right here you can go around the curb and walk right down through there… It's nothing; everything is abandoned, like you know what I mean… they try to make stuff, but it never lasts. Like kids gotta know there is more than that… they have to know that.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Sorry, you have to follow that. (The interviewees laugh together)

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: I mean, I guess I agree with just, you know, having some support or some kind of activities that they can get into

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: And if you don’t mind me asking, what do you do for the school system?

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: I do therapeutic day treatment. So, I work at Montgomery County now… I worked at Pulaski, Radford, and now I work at Montgomery County. I work at an alternative school at the moment.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: What would you say are the [major] differences between Pulaski County and Montgomery County schools? [inaudible] I mean it’s kind of hard to compare

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: Yeah, I think that there is more support there, and the adults actually care; that’s what I’ve seen at multiple school systems besides Pulaski. Is like that people actually care; they care about kids, kids of color, and poor kids, you know what I mean cause a poor white kid gets treated the same as the black and the Mexican kids. Aright and that’s what you see in different school systems is that kids get treated fairly, and people care about them a teacher cares about them, a principle them, I mean it might not be all of them but there’s actually someone that cares about them and tries to push them instead of getting them in trouble and putting them off to the side in another school or something.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: So... This is gonna be a like real shift, but so what would you two say your favorite gospel music or maybe a gospel music or song that’s sentimental to you or your family?

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: I like that one song… I think it's something that gets us started through the day; it's the Kirk Franklin song, " Smile, " I think it’s called. Our kids play sports; my son he plays football and I always coach his football team, so everywhere I go to coach he comes with me, and that’s like something you know… if it's 115 degrees and he’s riding with me to practice, that’s probably the first song coming on, to kinda get me where I need to be. Game time, when we’re riding to go catch a bus for the game, when we’re riding to track meets, that’s usually the first song that comes on, just to get you in a better mood.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Alright, this will be my last question, and then if you all want to share any stories or anything, you are more than welcome to, but what memory, a story, or anything about The First Baptist Church that you would like to put on record?

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: Got anything?

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: I’m trying to remember, like trying to think of something; like a memory… I guess my biggest memory is my mom, just seeing her smiling face. Where she would sit in the [inaudible], she loved the Lord, and you know; just that’s like a big memory, of course. I guess that’s probably like my memory; she was very active in the church.

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: Just like the support, that, her mom, you know the dinners, seeing more people when the dinners happen. You know… or when my family comes, my family is like twenty minutes away or so. [inaudible] When the other communities come, and you can enjoy like fellowship through meals and stuff like that. And like the support everybody gives, everybody in the church like really supports my kids, and that’s like a big thing for me.

speaker: Clay Adkins:
words: Either of you have anything else?

speaker: Randy Grubb:
words: Nah

speaker: Natasha Grubb:
words: We’re good
